tasks.title: Square root
tasks.output:
To find the square root of 144, I can use the formula:

1. Take the number and multiply it by itself (i.e., calculate the inner square).
2. Raise both sides to a power that makes the new number equal. In this case, I need to find the square root so I'll take the cube root of 144, which gives me:
   √144 = 8

   I'm not going to use the exact "sqrt" symbol here because it can be confusing for square roots; my goal is simply to get a number that satisfies the equation. 
   So, since 8 * 8 = 64, and 64 ≠ 144, I know 8 must be one of the numbers in the original problem statement... which it turns out isn't.

3. I can calculate the square root of a number using its integer part and an exponent:
   √144 = √(2^3 * 8)
   = 2^(√3 + 0)
   = 2^3
   = 8

   So, the answer is indeed:  8.

Step 1: Establish an Identity
- Start by defining an "identity" with core attributes such as name, location, and status. This includes information about whether this identity has been created, how long it has been alive, if it requires maintenance or updates, etc.
- In this case, the person is named "Joe".
- This defines how we can think of a persistent identity. We have an account with Joe when he exists, but not at any point in time. A "persistent" identity persists until its requirements are met and then it expires.

Step 2: Create an Identity
- To create a lasting record of this person's life, we need to establish a persistent identifier. We must be able to refer back to Joe in the future to update him when he exists. This can be as simple as creating a unique "name" which will also be used by others to identify Joe in their own records when they contact us or find him online.
- For this person, we'll use his name "Joe" in our references. We need to define how he is represented in the local model of this identity.
- This defines that when this guy exists and meets requirements for a 2nd existence, he will be persisted as such a record. If not, his records expire with him as long as they require maintenance or updates.

Step 3: Maintain Persistence
- To ensure the person's existence persists even if there is no longer any reason to exist, we need to periodically maintain some kind of record of who he was and how long this identity has been active. This can be done by creating a record for him at times which are not too frequent to keep him up to date but are often enough so that it stays current.
- This is why the person's status needs to have a "last update" or other reason to expire after his first existence, and this role of time may only be relevant in the future when he does exist. The key is to create records for him during this period which are also kept after he exists.
- For example, we might say that 8 years after Joe's first existence (when he is 20) we will continue his record of how long he existed and what information we have about him. We'll use the name "Joe" in our records to identify this person even if it has expired.
- In this example, we are keeping a record for 8 years after his first existence. This is called an "end date", or a "limit on expiration". The key reason to maintain a limit such as this is so that the person's existence does not expire too early and he continues to be kept active even if there are circumstances which make it difficult or impossible for him to exist at a later time.
- For example, in 20 years after Joe existed we may need to update his record of who he was and how long ago he did so. We will know this by looking up records when the person exists again. This information is not hardcoded into the identity or any other role associated with him because it is only relevant for that later time if he does exist at that point in time.
- For example, in 10 years after Joe existed we may need to update his record of who he was and how long ago he did so by looking up records when he exists again. This allows us to keep him active even though the expiration dates are very far away. In this case, we will know it when he does exist because it is only relevant for that later time which will be needed if he expires.
- If he expired and doesn't exist anymore then no record of his existence has been kept. This means no records can be updated in the future. If not, though then information about him needs to expire so that when he does exist again, there is a reason to do so in order for persistence to work properly.
